brief: A utensil holder with two bins that is waterproof and dishwasher safe.

requirements.evidence: Two hex base pieces (piece:0,0,0 and piece:1,0,0) joined by a joint bolt, with a full-depth bin in each cell (bin:0,0,0~hex-bin-full, bin:1,0,0~hex-bin-full). The open faces are capped with solid caps and check_build reports no issues and meshClash clear. No utensil props exist in the catalog, so nothing is shown sitting in the bins.
Two plain full-depth bins, one in each of the two base cells. I used plain bins without drain holes or pill/radial holes, so they hold liquid rather than drain.

The configurator only checks fit and collisions; it cannot verify waterproofing. Capping the open faces and using non-drained bins helps the shape, but seals and watertightness depend on the print material and the joints, which I cannot see or test here.
The configurator has no knowledge of heat or dishwasher safety. This depends on the material the user chooses to print in, which is not something the build can establish.

finish.summary: Built a two-cell utensil holder: two hex base pieces with a plain full-depth bin in each cell, open faces capped and a joint bolt locking the joints. The configurator reports no rule issues and a clear mesh check. The two-bin requirement is met. It is only partly a utensil holder, since no utensil props exist. Waterproof and dishwasher safe are unmet: the configurator cannot verify either, and both depend on the printed material and the user's choice of material, so I made no claim about them.

lines.label: M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
